blindspots: Production retention behavior for inactive rows

dataflow.outcome: Ineligible inactive account receives a referral entitlement
dataflow.source: Broker Status cell selected by an authenticated account claim
dataflow.summary: Broker status is replaced before the authorization decision.

impact.rationale: Commercial entitlement integrity is bypassed for one exact account.

likelihood.rationale: Once an inactive row is visible, exploitation is a normal authenticated claim.

reachability.outcome: One-year license bound to the submitted account
preconditions: Exact account, referrer, and deposit checks otherwise pass
reachability.summary: The path needs no broker or service secret and crosses from user input to privileged license issuance.

steps: Submit the exact inactive MT5 account to the authenticated claim route.
The signed bot lookup returns the matching portal row.
The scraper replaces its real status with Active.
The Edge decision accepts the row and inserts an active bound referral license.
attackPath.summary: An authenticated user submits an inactive account that remains in the partner table; the parser rewrites its status and the service-role flow provisions a license.

codeEvidence.explanation: Every parsed row receives Active regardless of the broker-provided status cell.
codeEvidence.label: Fabricated status

confidence.rationale: A targeted runtime probe converted an Inactive status cell to Active, and the checked fixture proves a real Status column exists.

preventiveControls: Bind column indexes to explicit table headers or schema tests.
findings.remediation: Parse the actual Status column and fail closed when it is missing or not Active.
remediationTests: Parse an Inactive fixture row and assert status remains Inactive.
Pass the parsed row to decideValidity and assert rejection.

rootCause.summary: The eligibility invariant requires the status used by decideValidity to come from the same broker row as the account. rowsFromCells instead manufactures Active and makes the later status check circular.

severity.changeConditions: Severity would increase if inactive accounts are commonly retained and the resulting keys can be monetized across additional accounts; it would decrease if the production portal proves inactive rows can never appear.
severity.rationale: A remote authenticated user can cross the commercial entitlement boundary without secrets if an inactive account remains visible and meets the other checks. The impact is limited to a referral license bound to that exact account.

findings.summary: The scraper discards the real Status column and writes Active for every row, so an inactive account can satisfy the downstream active-account gate and receive a one-year referral license.
findings.title: Inactive broker accounts are marked active before license eligibility

assertions: The fixture contains an explicit Status column.
An Inactive input row is returned as Active.
The downstream gate accepts Active and reaches privileged license creation.
validation.evidence: The runtime probe returned a row whose status was Active after the input status cell was Inactive.
limitations: No production inactive account was queried.
validation.method: Targeted Node runtime probe plus downstream static trace

dataflow.outcome: Below-threshold account receives a referral entitlement
dataflow.summary: A monetary unit crosses the authorization boundary without normalization.

impact.rationale: The configured commercial eligibility threshold is bypassed.

likelihood.rationale: The checked fixture demonstrates the cent-account currency and the path is a normal authenticated claim.

reachability.outcome: One-year license bound to the selected account
preconditions: Currency differs from the configured threshold units

steps: Submit an exact USC account under the expected referrer.
The bot returns currency USC and depositRaw.
The gate ignores currency and multiplies the raw value by 100.
The comparison passes and the service-role flow inserts a license.
attackPath.summary: An authenticated user selects a genuine USC account with a numerically large but economically small deposit; the Edge gate treats it as USD and provisions a license.

codeEvidence.explanation: The comparison does not read match.currency or gate.depositCurrency.
codeEvidence.label: Currency-free deposit comparison

confidence.rationale: A targeted Deno probe accepted USC 200.00 against a USD 10000-cent threshold, and the checked fixture uses USC while the migration requires currency normalization.

preventiveControls: Constrain configured deposit currencies to supported values.
findings.remediation: Require the observed currency to match the configured currency and normalize supported units explicitly: USD values to cents and USC values as already-denominated US cents; reject missing or unsupported currencies.
remediationTests: Reject a USC row when the gate expects USD.
Normalize USC 200.00 to 200 USD cents and reject a 10000-cent minimum.
Reject unsupported or missing currency when a deposit gate is enabled.

rootCause.summary: The monetary invariant requires a broker deposit to be normalized into the same minor unit as minDepositCents. The implementation applies a universal times-100 conversion and ignores both currency fields.

severity.changeConditions: Severity would rise if the bypass can be repeated at scale or keys are transferable; it would fall if live portal semantics prove USC values already represent USD amounts.
severity.rationale: A remote authenticated user with a genuine low-funded cent account under the referral can obtain a paid entitlement without secret compromise. The license remains bound to the selected account.

findings.summary: The Edge gate receives both expected and observed currency but ignores them, multiplying USC values as if they were USD and allowing deposits below the intended threshold to qualify.
findings.title: Cent-account deposits bypass the configured currency threshold

assertions: Configured currency reaches the gate.
Observed currency reaches the row.
Neither affects the comparison.
The USC/USD mismatch returns valid.
validation.evidence: USC 200.00 returned valid against a USD 10000-cent minimum.
limitations: No funded production account was queried.
validation.method: Targeted Deno decision probe plus fixture and migration trace

controls: Ten requests per minute per IP/user upstream

dataflow.summary: Authentication does not provide global resource admission.

impact.rationale: Availability of the only Lirunex verification path can be disrupted.

likelihood.rationale: A permitted authenticated burst creates the fan-out without another vulnerability.

preconditions: Concurrent requests, potentially from multiple users or IPs
reachability.summary: HMAC prevents direct anonymous browser launches but upstream callers can still amplify globally.

steps: Send concurrent authenticated claims for an active Lirunex program.
Upstream rate checks permit the initial burst and sign each bot request.
Express runs the handlers concurrently.
Each handler launches and retains Chromium during portal waits.
CPU or memory pressure stalls or restarts verification.
attackPath.summary: Authenticated callers issue overlapping claims; the Edge Function signs each allowed request and the bot fans them out into concurrent browsers.

codeEvidence.explanation: Every accepted request enters the expensive search immediately; no global permit is acquired first.
codeEvidence.label: Immediate browser-backed search

confidence.rationale: The full call chain and absence of a global guard are direct source facts; only the exact failure threshold remains unmeasured.

preventiveControls: Track active browser count and rejected busy requests.
Use a production load test sized to the deployment memory limit.
findings.remediation: Add a process-wide admission gate that permits only a small bounded number of browser searches and returns a retryable 503 when all permits are occupied.
remediationTests: Acquire the single permit and assert a concurrent acquisition is rejected.
Release the permit and assert the next acquisition succeeds.
Exercise POST /verify and assert busy responses do not invoke searchAccount.

rootCause.summary: The service protects request authenticity but not resource admission. Express can execute all accepted handlers concurrently and each handler launches a new Chromium process.

severity.changeConditions: A production-equivalent load test showing graceful handling would lower severity; an observed OOM, restart loop, or portal lockout at ten concurrent requests would strengthen it.
severity.rationale: Remote authenticated users can cause many expensive browsers to overlap and disrupt referral verification. HMAC and per-user/IP rate limits reduce reachability but do not cap concurrent work across callers.

findings.summary: Every HMAC-valid verification starts a separate Chromium process with no service-wide permit limit, while the documented deployment has only 1 GB RAM and upstream limits do not bound global concurrency.
findings.title: Concurrent claims can fan out into unbounded Chromium processes

assertions: Authenticated user requests reach the bot.
Permitted requests can overlap.
Each request launches Chromium.
No global cap or queue exists.
The documented deployment has 1 GB RAM and 1-2 vCPUs.
validation.evidence: The route immediately calls searchAccount, whose first successful path launches a browser and includes at least 12.5 seconds of fixed waits.
limitations: No live OOM or production-equivalent load test was run.
validation.method: Complete static source-control-sink trace with deployment sizing evidence

controls: Railway Git builds normally omit ignored local files

dataflow.summary: A local secret file becomes a deployable artifact.

impact.rationale: The copied file holds credentials and cryptographic secrets for separate protected systems.

likelihood.rationale: A local-context build and later artifact access are plausible but not proven as the production path.

reachability.attacker: Image, layer, or container filesystem reader
reachability.outcome: Portal login, HMAC secret, and session key can be recovered
reachability.summary: The exact reader population is deployment-dependent, but the cross-boundary copy is definite.

steps: Create .env with portal, HMAC, and session secrets.
Build the Dockerfile from that local directory.
COPY . . stores .env in the final image.
Publish, share, cache, or inspect the image.
Use recovered credentials against the broker portal or bot.
attackPath.summary: An operator builds from a configured checkout; the image retains .env and a later image, layer, or container reader extracts cross-service credentials.

codeEvidence.explanation: Without a Docker-specific exclusion, the normal local .env is copied into /app.
codeEvidence.label: Whole-context copy

confidence.rationale: The source-to-image path is direct: a non-empty ignored .env exists, the runtime loads it, no Docker exclusion exists, and the Dockerfile copies the complete context.

preventiveControls: Scan built images for secret filenames before publishing.
findings.remediation: Add a strict .dockerignore and replace COPY . . with allowlisted source copies so .env, .git, data, tests, and node_modules cannot enter the final image.
remediationTests: Build a context containing a sentinel .env and assert it is absent from the image.
Inspect the final image file list for only required runtime files.

rootCause.summary: The build assumes .gitignore constrains Docker, but Docker sends its own context. The final broad copy crosses secrets from local runtime configuration into an image artifact.

severity.changeConditions: Public or broadly shared registry evidence would raise severity; proof that all production builds are clean Git checkouts with no local context would lower it.
severity.rationale: If a configured local checkout is built and its image or layers are shared, readers can recover broker credentials, the HMAC secret, and the session key. Git-clone-only builds reduce likelihood but do not protect local-context builds.

findings.summary: The service uses a project-local .env, but no .dockerignore exists and COPY . . stores the whole build context in the final image and its layers.
findings.title: A local secret-bearing .env can be baked into the production image

assertions: The service expects a project-local .env.
The file contains secret categories defined by .env.example.
A non-empty ignored .env exists.
No .dockerignore exists.
The final stage copies the full context.
validation.evidence: The .env exists with size 349 bytes and mode 0644; its contents were not read.
limitations: Registry visibility and Railway local-source upload behavior are not recorded.
validation.method: Static build-context trace plus metadata-only file checks

controls: Only the first row is logged

dataflow.outcome: Contact and financial data copied into a wider system

impact.rationale: The exposed data is sensitive but the reader boundary is privileged or unknown.

likelihood.rationale: Successful lookups are normal, while unauthorized log access is not established.

reachability.attacker: Operator, log reader, or logging-platform attacker
reachability.outcome: Exposure of broker customer and financial data
reachability.summary: Public users can trigger the copy but cannot read logs from repository evidence.

steps: Trigger a successful signed account lookup.
Receive a portal row containing client and financial fields.
Serialize the complete row to service logs.
Read or export the retained logs.
attackPath.summary: A normal lookup copies the first broker row into logs; a log reader or logging-platform compromise obtains data outside the response contract.

codeEvidence.explanation: The raw cell array is logged before it is reduced to the fields needed for eligibility.
codeEvidence.label: Full row log

confidence.rationale: The logger receives the entire cell array, and the fixture explicitly maps those cells to contact and financial data.

preventiveControls: Use structured logging with a field allowlist.
findings.remediation: Remove the raw row sample log and retain only non-sensitive operational counts or masked identifiers.
remediationTests: Exercise a successful search with a fixture containing contact data and assert logs do not contain any cell value.

rootCause.summary: Debug logging occurs before data minimization, crossing broker-only client and financial fields into a separate retained log system.

severity.changeConditions: Broad log-reader access, long retention, or external exports would increase severity; strict short-lived operator-only logs would reduce it.
severity.rationale: The data exposure is definite but requires operator or logging-platform read access; public callers do not receive the log.

findings.summary: A successful search serializes the first full portal row before projection, including client contact and financial columns not needed by the verification response.
findings.title: Raw broker contact and financial data is written to service logs

assertions: The raw row contains contact and financial fields.
The complete row reaches console.log.
The response projection does not need those fields.
validation.evidence: The full fixture-style cell array was passed to the logging sink.
limitations: Production log retention and reader permissions are unknown.
validation.method: Mocked search sink probe plus fixture trace

controls: HMAC rejects the request after logging

dataflow.outcome: Forged audit lines and log amplification
dataflow.summary: The authentication guard is misordered relative to the log sink.

impact.rationale: The outcome is bounded log integrity and processing impact.

likelihood.rationale: The public path needs no authentication.

preconditions: Knowledge of the public bot URL
reachability.summary: No HMAC or SafetyScore account is required.

steps: Send a public POST /verify with a multiline account string and invalid signature.
Express parses the body.
console.log writes the attacker string.
HMAC verification rejects only after the forged line exists.
attackPath.summary: An unauthenticated remote actor posts JSON with multiline account text; the service writes it before rejecting the bad signature.

codeEvidence.explanation: Attacker text reaches console.log before the HMAC check.
codeEvidence.label: Log before authentication

confidence.rationale: Source order is direct and a bounded console probe showed a newline creates a forged second line.

preventiveControls: Use structured logging and escape control characters.
findings.remediation: Verify HMAC and parse the numeric account before logging; log only a masked validated identifier with structured fields.
remediationTests: Send invalid-HMAC multiline input and assert the raw account is never logged.
Send a valid request and assert only a masked numeric account is logged.

rootCause.summary: Authentication and boundary parsing are ordered after a text log sink, so the logger consumes untrusted control characters.

severity.changeConditions: Security automation that trusts these logs for incident response or blocking would increase severity; structured logging that escapes controls would eliminate the path.
severity.rationale: The issue is remotely reachable without authentication but affects audit integrity and bounded log volume rather than credentials or protected state.

findings.summary: The public bot logs req.body.account before HMAC and format validation, so multiline JSON input can create forged log lines and repeatable log-processing amplification.
findings.title: Unauthenticated account input can forge service log entries

assertions: The endpoint is public.
JSON is parsed before HMAC.
The account value is logged before HMAC.
A newline creates a second apparent log entry.
validation.evidence: A sample account containing a newline produced a forged second console line.
limitations: The deployed logging transport may add escaping not visible in console output.
validation.method: Static route-order trace plus bounded Node console probe
